title: Process mining in practice: Disco and Apromore case studies

cards.question: What are the four stages of the process mining analysis roadmap used in the Disco tutorial?
cards.answer: Questions, data extraction, data analysis and presentation.
distractors: Modelling, simulation, execution and monitoring.
Discovery, conformance, enhancement and prediction.
Data cleaning, feature engineering, training and deployment.

cards.question: What is determined in the 'Questions' stage of the roadmap?
cards.answer: The questions to answer, the scope of the process, and which IT systems are involved.
distractors: The final process model to be discovered.
The thresholds of the dependency measure.
The layout of the final report.

cards.question: In the roadmap, how is data typically obtained in the data extraction stage?
cards.answer: Via the database administrator or IT staff, as a CSV file or database extract of history logs from the system.
distractors: By manually drawing the process on a whiteboard.
By interviewing every employee about each case.
By generating synthetic logs from a Petri net.

cards.question: What is done in the data analysis stage of the roadmap?
cards.answer: Extracting the 'as-is' process and answering the questions posed at the start.
distractors: Choosing which IT system to log.
Presenting the results in a workshop.
Defining the scope of the process.

cards.question: What is the difference between the data analysis stage and the presentation stage of the roadmap?
cards.answer: Analysis extracts the as-is process and answers the questions; presentation communicates the results, for example in a report, presentation or workshop.
distractors: Analysis communicates the results; presentation extracts the data.
Analysis defines the scope; presentation selects the IT systems.
They are two names for the same stage.

cards.question: What is the example scenario in the Disco tutorial?
cards.answer: A purchasing process supported by an ERP system, involving requester, requester manager, purchasing agent, supplier and financial manager.
distractors: A hospital treating sepsis patients.
A telephone repair process.
A refund process of an electronics manufacturer.

cards.question: Which three problems motivate the purchasing case study?
cards.answer: Inefficient operations, the need to demonstrate compliance, and complaints about process duration.
distractors: Missing event logs, noise and incomplete cases.
Lack of IT staff, expensive licenses and unreadable data.
High error rates in the data extraction only.

cards.question: What are the three analysis goals of the purchasing case study?
cards.answer: Understand the process in detail, check for deviations from the payment guidelines, and control performance targets (21 days).
distractors: Predict future purchases, price suppliers and optimize inventory.
Discover a Petri net, check soundness and compute reachability.
Cluster customers, rank suppliers and detect fraud only.

cards.question: What does each row of disco-log.csv correspond to?
cards.answer: One event, with its case ID, activity, start and end times, resource and role.
distractors: One case with all its activities in one cell.
One activity type with its frequency.
One resource with its workload.

cards.question: How are the columns mapped when importing the purchasing log into Disco?
cards.answer: Case ID → Case ID; start and complete timestamps → Timestamp; Activity → Activity; Resource → Resource; Role → Other.
distractors: Role → Case ID; Resource → Activity; Timestamp → Other.
Activity → Case ID; Case ID → Activity.
All columns → Other.

cards.question: In Disco's process map, what do the numbers in the rectangles and on the arcs mean?
cards.answer: Numbers in rectangles are activity frequencies; numbers on arcs are the frequencies of the connections.
distractors: Numbers in rectangles are mean durations; numbers on arcs are resources.
Numbers in rectangles are case IDs; numbers on arcs are timestamps.
Numbers in rectangles are the dependency measure; numbers on arcs are noise levels.

cards.question: How many cases are in the purchasing log, and with which activity do they all start?
cards.answer: 608 cases, all starting with 'Create Purchase Requisition'.
distractors: 9,119 cases, all starting with 'Create Request for Quotation'.
1,104 cases, starting with various activities.
1,050 cases, all starting with 'Admission'.

cards.question: What do the 'Activities' and 'Paths' sliders in Disco do?
cards.answer: They adjust the level of detail of the process map: how many activities and how many paths (arcs) are shown.
distractors: They set the time window of the log.
They choose the resources to display.
They change the case ID column.

cards.question: What does the process map show when the Activities slider is at 0%?
cards.answer: Only the activities of the most frequent process variant.
distractors: Only the activities with the longest durations.
All activities, without arcs.
Only start and end activities of all variants.

cards.question: In the purchasing map, 11 cases flow into 'Amend Purchase Requisition' but only 8 flow out at 100% activities but with fewer paths. Where are the other 3?
cards.answer: They move to 'Create Request for Quotation', a path hidden by the Paths slider, visible when the slider is at 100%.
distractors: They are deleted from the log as noise.
They end the process after the amendment.
They move to 'Release Supplier's Invoice'.

cards.question: Why is it important to adjust the level of detail of a process map?
cards.answer: The full map can be unreadable (spaghetti), while the simplified one shows the main flow; being able to move between them avoids missing infrequent but relevant paths.
distractors: Only the simplified map is correct.
Only the full map is correct.
Level of detail changes the event log.

cards.question: What does the 'Statistics' tab of the purchasing log show?
cards.answer: 9,119 events for 608 cases, covering January to October 2011, with most cases lasting up to about 15–16 days and some more than 70–80 days.
distractors: 1,104 events for 9 cases in 2019.
1,050 patients treated within 1.37 weeks.
608 events for 9,119 cases in 2011.

cards.question: What does the 'Cases' tab in Disco show?
cards.answer: The process variants and individual cases of the log.
distractors: The resources and their roles only.
The model quality measures.
The Petri net of the process.

cards.question: What is a process variant?
cards.answer: A distinct sequence of activities that is followed by one or more cases.
distractors: A different version of the process model.
A different process owner.
A different timestamp of the same event.

cards.question: In the purchasing log, the third most frequent variant ends after 'Analyze Purchase Requisition' (about 10.36% of cases). What question does this raise?
cards.answer: Why are so many requests stopped, for example do people not know what they are allowed to buy?
distractors: Why do all cases finish successfully?
Why is the supplier slow?
Why are payments doubled?

cards.question: What are the findings of the purchasing discovery step?
cards.answer: The process map shows lots of amendments and stopped requests, so the purchasing guidelines need to be updated.
distractors: The process contains no deviations.
The process is purely sequential.
All cases are completed within 21 days.

cards.question: How is a performance filter used to check the 21-day target?
cards.answer: Add a Performance filter with 21 days as lower bound to keep only cases that take longer; about 15% (92 cases) are longer.
distractors: Delete all cases shorter than 21 days from the log permanently.
Filter by resource to remove slow people.
Filter by activity names containing 21.

cards.question: How many of the 608 purchasing cases take longer than 21 days, and what is typical for them?
cards.answer: 92 cases (about 15%), with on average 3 amendments per case.
distractors: 243 cases, with 1 amendment per case.
10 cases, which skip the invoice release.
1,104 cases, with 2 repairs each.

cards.question: What does Disco's Performance view with 'Total duration' show, in contrast to 'Mean duration'?
cards.answer: Total duration shows the high-impact areas (time summed over all cases); mean duration shows how long it takes on average per occurrence.
distractors: Total duration shows the shortest paths; mean duration the longest ones.
Total duration shows resources; mean duration shows activities.
They show the same values.

cards.question: In the slow purchasing cases, how long does it take on average to return from the rework loop to the normal process?
cards.answer: More than 14 days.
distractors: About 14 minutes.
About 2 days.
About 70–80 days.

cards.question: Which activity is identified as the big bottleneck in the purchasing process?
cards.answer: 'Analyze Request for Quotation'.
distractors: 'Create Purchase Requisition'.
'Release Supplier's Invoice'.
'Repair (complex)'.

cards.question: What is the purpose of Disco's process animation?
cards.answer: To visualize how cases move through the process over time, with the most used paths getting thicker, which shows bottlenecks.
distractors: To generate the Petri net of the process.
To simulate future cases with random durations.
To remove noise from the log.

cards.question: How is the compliance check done in the purchasing case?
cards.answer: Remove the performance filter, look at the end of the frequency map, and then filter the suspicious path to inspect the cases.
distractors: Compute the dependency measure for every pair of activities.
Count the number of resources.
Use the alpha algorithm to discover a Petri net.

cards.question: What compliance violation is found in the purchasing log?
cards.answer: 10 cases skip the mandatory activity 'Release Supplier's Invoice' before authorizing the payment.
distractors: 10 cases skip 'Create Purchase Requisition'.
92 cases skip the invoice release.

cards.question: How is the compliance violation of the 10 cases isolated in Disco?
cards.answer: By clicking the path from 'Send invoice' to 'Authorize Supplier's Invoice payment' and using 'Filter this path…', then looking at the Cases view.
distractors: By deleting the activity 'Release Supplier's Invoice'.
By sorting the log by resources.
By changing the Case ID column.

cards.question: What actions can follow the compliance finding?
cards.answer: Either change the operational system to prevent the violation, or provide targeted training.
distractors: Delete the cases from the log.
Raise the dependency threshold.
Remove the activity from the model.

cards.question: How is the organizational view created in Disco?
cards.answer: Reload the project, set the 'Activity' column to 'Other' and configure the 'Role' column as 'Activity'.
distractors: Set the Case ID column to Resource.
Filter the log by role.
Switch to Statistics view.

cards.question: What does the organizational view of the process show?
cards.answer: How the process flows between roles in the organization, where inefficiencies are often found at the borders between organizational units.
distractors: The shortest path of each case.
Only the frequency of activities.
The number of events per day.

cards.question: Which role causes the biggest delays in the purchasing process according to the organizational view?
cards.answer: The purchasing agents.
distractors: The requesters.
The suppliers.
The financial managers.

cards.question: What does 'closing the loop' mean in the Disco tutorial?
cards.answer: After analysis, take action to improve the process and then verify the results, for example by mining new data.
distractors: Adding a loop to the process model.
Closing the log after the last event.
Deleting finished cases from the log.

cards.question: What are the take-away points of the Disco tutorial?
cards.answer: Real processes are more complex than expected; there is no single 'right' model, as you can take multiple views on the same data; and process mining is an explorative, interactive activity.
distractors: Real processes are always simple.
There is exactly one correct model per log.
Process mining is a fully automatic, one-shot activity.

cards.question: What is the typical tool-based discovery exercise on the L2 log (health insurance claims) in Apromore?
cards.answer: Discover a BPMN model automatically, using Discover → Discover model on the selected log.
distractors: Compute reachability graphs of Petri nets.
Fit a regression to claim durations.
Filter the log to cases with complaints.

cards.question: What is the difference between waiting time and processing time of an activity?
cards.answer: Waiting time is the time between the previous activity and the start of this one; processing time is the time spent executing the activity itself.
distractors: Waiting time is the duration of the activity; processing time is the time between cases.
